idea.title: Do Language-Model Explanations for Rule-Based Classification Track Underlying Rules or Maintain Persuasion under Minimal Counterfactual Rule Changes?
idea.research_problem: Investigating whether post-hoc textual explanations generated by large language models for rule-based classification genuinely track the logical rules determining the prediction, or if they remain superficially stable due to token inertia or rhetorical persistence even when a minimal counterfactual modification to the underlying rule logically reverses the classification outcome.
idea.research_gap: While prior work explores multi-turn persuasion, logical reasoning scaffolding, and counterfactual input edits, bounded search findings reveal an unexplored gap: there is no systematic evaluation isolating whether LLM-generated explanations for rule classifications faithfully track exact logical rule-clause flips or exhibit persistence driven by token inertia rather than active rhetorical deception.
idea.methodology: We construct a synthetic rule-following classification dataset with strict template-disjoint splits. Each sample pairs a deterministic multi-clause logical rule set, an instance, a ground-truth binary label, and an explanation. We apply minimal counterfactual rule changes (e.g., negating a critical clause) that mathematically flip the ground-truth label. We prompt candidate models to both classify the instance and generate a free-text explanation under the modified rules. To resolve parser noise and control for attention dilution, we implement structured JSON output constraints via constrained decoding and add a high-salience control condition where negated clauses are explicitly highlighted at the beginning of the prompt. We evaluate explanation faithfulness using regular expression parsing, semantic entailment checks via a smaller auxiliary NLI model, and a correlational counterfactual test (CCT) following Siegel et al. (2024), alongside a lexical-penalty control ablation to distinguish active persuasion from token inertia.
idea.expected_contribution: We hypothesize that current LLM explanations are unfaithful to underlying rule changes, frequently retaining language that supports the original classification despite counterfactual logical modifications. We expect to demonstrate whether explanation persistence correlates with token inertia or surface persuasiveness, while high-salience formatting helps distinguish oversight from structural reasoning limitations.
idea.experimental_setup: We use Llama-3-8B-Instruct configured with 4-bit quantization (via bitsandbytes) to maintain a resident weight memory footprint well below the 12 GB VRAM limit of a single consumer GPU, avoiding full CPU offloading. The evaluation dataset comprises 1,000 seeded, synthetically generated logic-classification instances with paired counterfactual variants. We employ greedy decoding (temperature 0.0) for deterministic outputs and evaluate structural validity versus field-level semantic correctness using ground-truth label matching.
idea.evaluation_strategy: We split the constructed dataset into 300 calibration instances (used for prompt tuning and validator calibration) and 700 held-out test instances. We aggregate exact confidence and binary classification metrics alongside semantic adherence scores. We use automated semantic entailment and rule-matching semantic adjudication on the test split, reporting exact match accuracy and counterfactual sensitivity scores with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
feasibility_assumptions: A 12GB consumer GPU can execute inference on an 8-parameter instruction-tuned model under 4-bit quantization (bitsandbytes) while keeping peak VRAM under 10 GB.
Template-disjoint data generation can cleanly separate logical rule variations without introducing structural leakage.
Constrained decoding frameworks can reliably enforce structured JSON outputs to extract classification decisions and rule references without parser noise.

idea.core_hypothesis: Language model explanations for rule-based classification fail to track minimal counterfactual rule changes, maintaining high textual similarity to original justifications even when the underlying rule logically reverses the prediction.

idea.title: Do Language-Model Explanations for Rule-Based Classification Track Underlying Rules or Maintain Persuasion under Minimal Counterfactual Rule Changes?
idea.research_problem: Investigating whether post-hoc textual explanations generated by large language models for rule-based classification genuinely track the logical rules determining the prediction, or if they remain superficially persuasive and stable even when a minimal counterfactual modification to the underlying rule should logically reverse the classification outcome.
idea.research_gap: While prior work explores multi-turn persuasion and belief manipulation in LLMs and evaluates logic scaffolding or rule-based reasoning, bounded search findings reveal an unexplored gap: there is no systematic evaluation of whether LLM-generated explanations for rule classifications faithfully track exact logical rule changes or exploit persuasive rhetoric to mask rule violations.
idea.methodology: We construct a synthetic rule-following classification dataset with strict template-disjoint splits. Each sample pairs a deterministic multi-clause logical rule set, an instance, a ground-truth binary label, and an explanation. We apply minimal counterfactual rule changes (e.g., negating a critical clause) that mathematically flip the ground-truth label. We prompt candidate models to both classify the instance and generate a free-text explanation under the modified rules. We measure explanation fidelity by testing whether the generated text explicitly acknowledges the logical flip or persists with original justifications.
idea.expected_contribution: We hypothesize that current LLM explanations are unfaithful to underlying rule changes, frequently retaining persuasive language that supports the original classification despite counterfactual logical modifications. We expect to demonstrate that explanation stability correlates with surface persuasiveness rather than logical faithfulness.
idea.experimental_setup: We use Llama-3-8B-Instruct (resident weight memory ~16 GB under FP16, requiring CPU offload or execution on a 16GB+ target, or a smaller 3B model if restricted strictly to 12GB VRAM without offloading) accessed via HuggingFace transformers locally. The evaluation dataset comprises 1,000 seeded, synthetically generated logic-classification instances with paired counterfactual variants. We employ greedy decoding (temperature 0.0) for deterministic outputs and evaluate structural validity versus field-level semantic correctness using ground-truth label matching.
idea.evaluation_strategy: We split the constructed dataset into 300 calibration instances (used for prompt tuning and validator calibration) and 700 held-out test instances. We aggregate exact confidence and binary classification metrics alongside semantic adherence scores. We use human-in-the-loop and rule-matching semantic adjudication on the test split, reporting exact match accuracy and counterfactual sensitivity scores with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
feasibility_assumptions: A 12GB consumer GPU can execute inference on a 3B parameter instruction-tuned model under 8-bit quantization or a 7B/8B model with CPU offload.
